lessons.readme:
# Welcome to Pandas

[Pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/) is Python's go-to library for working with tables of data, like spreadsheets, CSV files, and database results.

![pandas and polars logos](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/APzv1tQ-1280x533.png)

A Pandas [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.html) represents one column, and the easiest way to make one is to simply convert from a Python list:

```py
temperatures = [42.0, 69.69, 9000]
temperature_series = pd.Series(temperatures)
```

## Assignment

During this course, you'll work on **SnackStack**, a fictional platform for collecting data from smart kitchen devices. SnackStack collects temperature readings from smart ovens, but there's a typo in the code!

**Fix the name of the [`pd.Series()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.html) call**, then run and submit the code.

files.name: main.py
files.content:
import pandas as pd

temperatures = [37.8, 121.0, 22.5]
temperature_series = pd.Serie(temperatures)

print(temperature_series)

lessons.readme:
# Data Types

Raw data is often given to you ~~from the marketing team~~ with the wrong types! For example, numbers as strings can't directly be used in calculations:

```py
grade_strings = pd.Series(["99.8", "95.0", "81.5"])
```

The handy Pandas [`.astype()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.astype.html) converts every value in a `Series`, so we can use it to quickly get _actual_ floats:

```py
grade_floats = grade_strings.astype(float)
```

## Assignment

**Complete the `convert_temperatures` function.** Create a Pandas [`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.html) from the `temperatures` list, convert its values to floats, and return it.

]

submit_cases = [pytest.param(*case, marks=pytest.mark.submit) for case in submit_cases]


@pytest.mark.parametrize(("temperatures", "expected"), run_cases + submit_cases)
def test_convert_temperatures(temperatures: list[str], expected: pd.Series) -> None:
    print("\n---------------------------------")
    print(f"Temperatures: {temperatures}")
    print(f"Expected:\n{expected}")
    actual = convert_temperatures(temperatures)
    print(f"Actual:\n{actual}")
    assert isinstance(actual, pd.Series)
    assert actual.equals(expected)

lessons.title: Extracting Data
lessons.readme:
# Extracting Data

Data work can get messy _fast_, so a reliable workflow often uses 7 stages:

1. **Extract** the raw data.
2. **Inspect** its shape and types.
3. **Clean** errors and inconsistencies.
4. **Transform** it into a useful structure.
5. **Aggregate** records into summaries.
6. **Analyze** the results.
7. **Deliver** the answer.

![Workflow Explainer](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/Workflow-1920x1080.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

Let's practice **extracting** readings from a raw string. Python's [`str.split()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.split) method splits a string into a list using the provided separator:

```py
raw_statuses = "true,false,false,true"
status_strings = raw_statuses.split(",")
# ["true", "false", "false", "true"]
```

## Assignment

**Fix the bug in the `extract_statuses` function.**

Pass `","` to the [`str.split()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.split) call so each status becomes its own string. The rest of the provided function converts them to booleans and returns a Pandas `Series`.

lessons.title: Dates and Times
lessons.readme:
# Dates and Times

Dates are deceptively tricky. They look simple, but they are _not_. Fortunately, Python has a [`datetime` module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html) built into the standard library, which offers tools for working with dates.

In real datasets, you'll find:

- Different date formats
- Missing time zones
- Weird offsets
- Inconsistent timestamps
- Business logic like "last 30 days" or "next business week"

... and it's up to _you_ to figure out how to handle it.

## Parsing Timestamps

You'll often receive a timestamp as a string:

```py
timestamp = "2026-05-28 14:30:00"
```

Which you'll then convert to a [`datetime` object](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime-objects) using [`datetime.strptime()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime.strptime):

```py
from datetime import datetime

timestamp = datetime.strptime("2026-05-28 14:30:00", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
print(timestamp)
# 2026-05-28 14:30:00
```

The `timestamp` here is an actual `datetime` object, not just a string. You can do math with it, compare it to other dates, etc.

That [format string](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#strftime-and-strptime-format-codes), `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"`, tells Python how to parse the text as a date and time:

- `%Y` = 4-digit year
- `%m` = month
- `%d` = day
- `%H` = hour in 24-hour time
- `%M` = minute
- `%S` = second

## Mixture of Formats

Different sources will often hand you different stringified date and time formats:

```py
iso_date = datetime.strptime("2024-01-15", "%Y-%m-%d")
us_date = datetime.strptime("01/15/2024", "%m/%d/%Y")
eu_date = datetime.strptime("15/01/2024", "%d/%m/%Y")
```

If the format string doesn't match the text exactly, parsing fails, and that's why dates are such a common cleaning problem.

> [!warning]
> The standard library makes working with dates and times _bearable_, but they're still annoying. For more complex pipelines, you'll eventually lean on tools like Pandas, [`dateutil`](https://dateutil.readthedocs.io/en/stable/), or [`zoneinfo`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/zoneinfo.html)... more on that later.

## Assignment

SnackStack's smart appliances send event timestamps as strings... guh.

**Complete the `parse_reading_timestamp` function.** It accepts a timestamp string and returns a `datetime` object.

Parse the timestamp with [`datetime.strptime()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime.strptime) using the format string `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"`.

> [!tip]
> The incoming timestamp string looks like `"2022-02-22 02:22:22"`.

lessons.readme:
# Datetime Math

Once you've parsed a date or timestamp, you usually want to _do_ something with it. You might want to know:

- How long has an order been in transit?
- When should the package arrive?

That's where [`timedelta`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#timedelta-objects) comes in.

> [!miriah]
> Working with data is all about _answering real questions_. You can't do data work without a goal in mind, or you'll just be shuffling numbers around.

## Date Difference

Subtract one [`datetime`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime-objects) from another and you get a `timedelta`:

```py
order_placed = datetime(2026, 5, 25, 14, 30, 0)
delivered_at = datetime(2026, 5, 29, 14, 30, 0)
difference = delivered_at - order_placed  # difference is a timedelta object
print(difference.days)  # the .days is... exactly what you expect
# 4
```

## Adding Time

You can also add or subtract a `timedelta` from a `datetime` to get a new `datetime`:

```py
order_placed = datetime(2026, 5, 25, 14, 30, 0)
expected_by = order_placed + timedelta(hours=6)
print(expected_by)
# 2026-05-25 20:30:00
```

## Assignment

SnackStack considers a device's reading "stale" if it stays quiet for too long.

**Complete the `calculate_stale_time` function.** It accepts a "reading_time" `datetime` and the maximum number of hours the device can stay silent, and returns a new `datetime` object representing the time when the reading will become stale.

Use the [`timedelta`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#timedelta-objects) function to add `max_silent_hours` to the reading timestamp and return the result.

lessons.title: Comparing Dates
lessons.readme:
# Comparing Dates

Sometimes you don't need to do date math; you just need to know which date comes first. Questions like:

- Was this book returned before its due date?
- Is this record inside the reporting window?
- Which event happened earliest?

Luckily, compatible [`datetime`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime-objects) values support normal comparison operators

## Basic Comparisons

You can compare two `datetime` values with operators like `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=`:

```py
returned_at = datetime(2026, 5, 15)
due_date = datetime(2026, 6, 1)

if returned_at < due_date:
    print("Book returned on time")
```

Which comes in handy whenever you want to _filter a dataset by date_.

## Sorting Dates

You can also sort `datetime` values directly:

```py
dates = [datetime(2026, 3, 1), datetime(2026, 1, 1), datetime(2026, 2, 1)]
dates.sort()
print(dates)
# [datetime.datetime(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0), datetime.datetime(2026, 2, 1, 0, 0), datetime.datetime(2026, 3, 1, 0, 0)]
```

## Assignment

SnackStack's ops team needs to know which appliances are overdue for a firmware update. Policy says a device must be updated within a certain number of minutes after its firmware was installed.

**Complete the `needs_firmware_update` function.** It accepts:

- `installed_at`: when the device's current firmware was installed
- `required_after_mins`: the number of minutes after installation that an update becomes required
- `checked_at`: the time of the compliance check

1. [ ] Calculate the update deadline by adding `required_after_mins` minutes to `installed_at` with a [`timedelta`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.timedelta).
2. [ ] Return `True` if the deadline is before `checked_at`, otherwise, return `False`.

lessons.title: List Comprehensions
lessons.readme:
# List Comprehensions

In data work, you're constantly building new lists. Say you have a list of songs:

```py
tracks = [
    {"track_id": "T-100", "plays": 2},
    {"track_id": "T-101", "plays": 5},
    {"track_id": "T-102", "plays": 4},
]
```

And you want a new list with just the number of "plays" for each track. You _can_ do that with a normal `for` loop:

```py
play_counts = []
for track in tracks:
    play_counts.append(track["plays"])
print(play_counts)
# [2, 5, 4]
```

It _works_, but it's a lot of boilerplate. Python gives us a shorter way with [list comprehensions](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#list-comprehensions).

```py
play_counts = [track["plays"] for track in tracks]
print(play_counts)
# [2, 5, 4]
```

It says:

- take `track["plays"]`
- for each `track`
- in the `tracks` list
- and give me a _new_ list with those values (`play_counts`)

The syntax is:

```py
[expression for item in iterable]
```

And if you want to _filter_ as well:

```py
[expression for item in iterable if condition]
```

For example:

```py
long_play_counts = [track["plays"] for track in tracks if track["plays"] > 3]
print(long_play_counts)
# [5, 4]
```

Not only are comprehensions more concise, but they're also often more performant than a normal loop because the Python interpreter can optimize them more easily under the hood.

> [!miriah]
> Just because you _can_ cram a **bunch** of logic into one massive comprehension doesn't mean you _should_. If it's too cursed, stick to a normal loop.

## Assignment

SnackStack's support team exports appliance support tickets as a list of dictionaries.

**Complete the `get_escalated_ticket_ids` function.** It accepts a list of ticket dictionaries and returns a list of ticket IDs. Use a list comprehension to create and return a list that:

1. [ ] Extracts just the `ticket_id` field from each dictionary
2. [ ] Includes only tickets with a `priority` of `4` or higher.
3. [ ] Includes only tickets with a `status` that is not "closed".

lessons.readme:
# Dictionary Comprehensions

If list comprehensions build lists, **dictionary comprehensions** build dictionaries. Say you have a list of game records:

```py
games = [
    {"game_id": "g-01", "title": "The Legend of Zelda", "status": "released"},
    {"game_id": "g-02", "title": "Half Life 3", "status": "delayed"},
    {"game_id": "g-03", "title": "Hades II", "status": "released"},
]
```

and want a dictionary where you can lookup `game_id` --> `title`. You can use a dictionary comprehension:

```py
game_titles = {game["game_id"]: game["title"] for game in games}
print(game_titles)
# {'g-01': 'The Legend of Zelda', 'g-02': 'Half Life 3', 'g-03': 'Hades II'}
```

To filter records while creating the dictionary, you can optionally add an `if` condition:

```py
released_titles = {
    game["game_id"]: game["title"] for game in games if game["status"] == "released"
}
print(released_titles)
# {'g-01': 'The Legend of Zelda', 'g-03': 'Hades II'}
```

So, to be precise, the syntax is:

```py
{key_expression: value_expression for item in iterable if condition}
```

## Assignment

1. [ ] Use each active device's `device_id` as the key.
2. [ ] Use that device's `model` as the value.
3. [ ] Exclude devices where `status` is not `"active"`.
4. [ ] Use a dictionary comprehension.

lessons.title: Data Formats
lessons.readme:
# Data Formats

Data providers pick the format that's convenient for _them_. As an analyst or engineer, you have the ~~pain~~ privilege of dealing with whatever shows up.

That usually means a small handful of formats over and over again. Some of the most common are:

- **[JSON](https://www.json.org/json-en.html)** for nested API data
- **[CSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comma-separated_values)** for plain tabular data
- **[Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/)** for compressed analytics data

## JSON

[JSON](https://www.json.org/json-en.html) is everywhere. It's the default format for many APIs because it's so easy to work with, and can represent nested data easily:

```json
{
  "user": {
    "name": "Alice",
    "id": 123
  },
  "class": "CS 140"
}
```

## CSV

[CSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comma-separated_values) is more common for tabular data. It's a simple text format where each **row is a record**, and each **column is a field**:

```csv
user,score
Alice,150
Bob,200
Lane,90000
Miriah,90001
```

## Parquet

[Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/) is a binary [columnar format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_orientation#Column-oriented) used in many larger analytics systems. You wouldn't open it in a text editor like CSV, but it's great for _massive_ datasets because it's:

- binary (not human-readable)
- commonly compressed
- typed
- columnar (data is stored by column instead of row, which can make analytics queries faster)

answers: Parquet for API responses; CSV for simple tabular reports; JSON for large datasets

lessons.title: Parsing JSON
lessons.readme:
# Parsing JSON

Almost every modern API gives you [JSON](https://www.json.org/json-en.html). Luckily, JSON maps nicely onto normal Python data structures:

- JSON objects become [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#dict)s
- JSON arrays become [`list`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#list)s

Python's built-in [`json.loads()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.loads) can convert a JSON string:

```py
json_string = '{"title": "The Matrix", "year": 1999}'
data = json.loads(json_string)

print(data["title"])
# The Matrix
print(data["year"])
# 1999
```

After that call, `data` is a normal Python dictionary that you can work with like any other.

## Nested Data

Real JSON is usually nested. You can drill down one level at a time with bracket notation:

```py
data = json.loads(
    '{"show": {"title": "Breaking Bad", "network": "AMC"}, "rating": {"score": 9.5}}'
)

print(data["show"]["title"])
# Breaking Bad
print(data["rating"]["score"])
# 9.5
```

Each pair of brackets goes one level deeper.

## Missing Keys

Real API data is messy, and sometimes you try to grab a value from a key that doesn't exist:

```py
data = {"title": "Breaking Bad"}

seasons = data["seasons"]
# raises KeyError: 'seasons'
```

Fortunately, the [`.get()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#dict.get) method lets you handle that case gracefully. It returns `None` if the key doesn't exist:

```py
seasons = data.get("seasons")
# seasons = None
```

Alternatively, you can provide a default value to return instead of `None`:

```py
seasons = data.get("seasons", 5)
# seasons = 5
```

> [!tip]
> Use bracket notation when a field _must_ exist. Use `.get()` when you're not sure and a default value is acceptable.

## Assignment

SnackStack's API returns device readings as JSON strings. Before the analytics team can use them, we need to parse the JSON and pull out _only_ the fields we care about.

**Complete the `parse_device_reading` function.** It accepts a JSON string and returns a dictionary with the reading details.

1. [ ] Parse the JSON string with [`json.loads()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.loads).
2. [ ] Return a new dictionary with these fields:
   1. [ ] `device_id`: from the `device` field's `id` field.
   2. [ ] `device_type`: from the `device` field's `type` field.
   3. [ ] `temperature`: from the `reading` field's `temperature` field.
   4. [ ] `battery_level`: from the `reading` field's _optional_ `battery_level` field Use the [`.get()` method](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#dict.get) so it defaults to `None` if the `battery_level` is missing.

> [!tip]
> You should `print()` the `json_string` manually to see what you're working with.

lessons.title: Variable-Depth JSON
lessons.readme:
# Variable-Depth JSON

Simple JSON access is easy:

```py
score = data["player"]["stats"]["score"]
```

The problem is that real API responses aren't always so predictable. Sometimes a field is nested 2 levels deep. Sometimes it's 4. Sometimes part of the path is missing entirely.

If you keep chaining [`.get()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#dict.get) over and over, the code can get... _unwieldy_.

## A Reusable Pattern

I like this helper function:

```py
from typing import Any


def extract_nested_value(data: dict[str, Any], *keys: str) -> Any | None:
    current = data
    for key in keys:
        if not isinstance(current, dict):
            return None
        current = current.get(key)
        if current is None:
            return None
    return current
```

It walks through a nested dictionary one key at a time, and if any key is missing, it returns `None` instead of crashing. Here's the usage:

```py
game_data = {"player": {"stats": {"score": 4500, "level": 12}}}

score = extract_nested_value(game_data, "player", "stats", "score")
# 4500
mana = extract_nested_value(game_data, "player", "stats", "mana")
# None (but no crash)
```

> [!tip]
> This isn't mandatory; it's just a clean way to avoid writing the same nested-access logic over and over.

## What `*keys` Means

The [`*keys` parameter](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#arbitrary-argument-lists) accepts _however many_ extra arguments are passed in and collects them into a tuple called `keys`. So in this call:

```py
extract_nested_value(game_data, "player", "stats", "score")
```

`keys` is:

```py
("player", "stats", "score")
```

## Assignment

SnackStack's smart appliances send telemetry as nested JSON.

**Complete the `get_device_temperature` function.** It accepts a device `json_string` and returns the nested temperature reading, a float, if available.

1. [ ] Parse the JSON string with [`json.loads()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.loads). If the JSON is invalid, catch the [`json.JSONDecodeError`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.JSONDecodeError) and return `None`.
2. [ ] Use `extract_nested_value` to fetch the value at the path `data` → `sensors` → `temperature`.
3. [ ] If the temperature value [is an instance of an `int` or `float`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#isinstance), return it as a float by wrapping it with the built-in [`float()` function](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#float).
4. [ ] Otherwise return `None`.

lessons.readme:
# Fetching JSON

So far, our JSON has been sitting there waiting for us. But in many cases, you'll need to go fetch it from an API first. If an API serves you JSON over HTTP, that means you'll:

1. Make a request
2. Read the response body
3. Parse the JSON

Python's built-in [`urllib.request` module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.request.html) can make simple HTTP requests.

```py
import urllib.request

url = "https://api.example.com/stocks"

with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response:
    raw_data = response.read()
    data = json.loads(raw_data)
```

- [`urlopen()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.request.html#urllib.request.urlopen) sends the request
- [`read()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/http.client.html#httpresponse-objects) gets the response body
- [`json.loads()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.loads) parses the JSON

## Assignment

**Complete the `fetch_device_status` function.** It accepts a `device_id` string and fetches its status (a dictionary) from the SnackStack API.

1. [ ] Build the test-only URL string using the given device ID:
   ```py
   f"https://api.snackstack.dev/devices/{device_id}/status"
   ```
2. [ ] Use [`urllib.request.urlopen()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.request.html#urllib.request.urlopen) to send the request.
3. [ ] Read the response body with [`.read()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/http.client.html#httpresponse-objects).
4. [ ] Parse the response body with [`json.loads()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.loads).
5. [ ] Return the parsed dictionary.
6. [ ] Catch [`urllib.error.URLError`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.error.html#urllib.error.URLError) for request failures or [`json.JSONDecodeError`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json.JSONDecodeError) for invalid JSON, and return `None` in either case.

lessons.readme:
# CSV Files

[CSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comma-separated_values) is the default "just export it to a file" data format.

It's simple, everywhere, and kind of _dumb_. That's not an insult; dumb formats are _useful_ formats because everyone understands them.

> [!miriah]
> If you do a lot of work with non-technical stakeholders, you'll work with CSVs via Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets _constantly_.

**This is what CSV data looks like:**

```csv
title,author,year
Dune,Frank Herbert,1965
The Hobbit,J.R.R. Tolkien,1937
Neuromancer,William Gibson,1984
```

Each line is a row, and rows are separated by newlines. Fields are separated by commas.

The first row _usually_ contains column names.

## Why CSV Is So Common

CSV sticks around because it's:

- Easy to export
- Easy to share
- Easy to open in any spreadsheet software
- Easy to parse in almost any programming language

One downside is that CSV has almost no built-in type information. Unlike JSON, **everything is text**.

## Reading a CSV File

Python's built-in [`csv` module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html) can parse CSV files using [`csv.DictReader`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictReader):

```py
import csv

with open("books.csv", "r", newline="") as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)
```

Each `row` comes back as a dictionary:

```py
{"title": "Dune", "author": "Frank Herbert", "year": "1965"}
```

## Working With Open Files

`csv.DictReader` expects a file-like object: something it can read text from one line at a time.

When you call [`open()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open), Python gives you a file object. `DictReader` reads from that and parses each CSV row as a dictionary.

Always use a [`with` statement](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#the-with-statement) when opening files. It closes the file automatically, even if something goes wrong. I also recommend setting `newline=""` when opening CSV files. This lets the `csv` module handle newlines itself, which avoids weird blank-line behavior on some systems.

## Loading Rows Into a List

If you want the _whole_ file in memory, you can build a list of dictionaries, one for each row:

```py
def load_book_data(filename: str) -> list[dict]:
    books = []
    with open(filename, "r", newline="") as file:
        reader = csv.DictReader(file)
        for row in reader:
            books.append(row)
    return books
```

## Assignment

SnackStack's device telemetry team exports sensor readings as CSV files. Let's make sure we can parse them.

1. [ ] **Complete the `load_device_readings` function.** It accepts a CSV file name and returns a list of dictionaries, one for each row.
   1. [ ] Open the file with a [`with`](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#the-with-statement) statement and `newline=""`.
   2. [ ] Use [`csv.DictReader`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictReader) to read each row as a dictionary.
   3. [ ] Return a list of those row dictionaries.
2. [ ] **Complete the `get_device_count` function.** It accepts a CSV file name and returns the number of devices in the file.
   1. [ ] Use your `load_device_readings` function to load the CSV.
   2. [ ] Return the length of the list.

lessons.title: CSV Type Conversion
lessons.readme:
# CSV Type Conversion

One of the biggest gotchas with [`csv.DictReader`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictReader) is that every value starts as a string. Even if a column _looks_ numeric, it's still parsed as plain text. Take this CSV snippet:

```csv
player,points_per_game,games_played
LeBron James,27.0,71
```

That row becomes this dictionary:

```py
{"player": "LeBron James", "points_per_game": "27.0", "games_played": "71"}
```

- `points_per_game` is a string
- `games_played` is _also_ a string (guh)

## Convert Values

If you want numbers, convert them explicitly:

```py
games_played = int(row["games_played"])
points_per_game = float(row["points_per_game"])
total_points = points_per_game * games_played
# 1917.0
```

## Wrong Types Break Code

If you forget to convert types, your code will crash, or it may behave incorrectly, which is arguably even worse! This crashes because Python can't compare a string to an integer:

```py
if row["games_played"] > 50:
    print("veteran season")
# TypeError: '>' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
```

Convert it to an `int` first:

```py
if int(row["games_played"]) > 50:
    print("veteran season")
```

> [!miriah]
> The worst thing is tweaking a long-running script because you missed a small runtime error. These small, testable changes like string-to-int conversions are everywhere – write tests for them.

2. [ ] Extract the `temperature` value from each row and convert it with [`float()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#float).
3. [ ] Return the average of those temperatures as a `float`.

# Filtering CSV Rows

CSV files often contain _way_ more rows than you need for the question you're answering. If you only want part of the file, filter rows by skipping them with [`continue`](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#break-and-continue-statements-and-else-clauses-on-loops) as you read them:

```py
with open("flights.csv", "r", newline="") as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    for row in reader:
        if row["on_time"] != "true":
            continue
        print(row["flight_number"])
```

In this example, only on-time flights make it to `print(row["flight_number"])`. If you need to do something later with the matching rows, append them to a list instead:

```py
delayed_flights = []
with open(filename, "r", newline="") as file:
    reader = csv.DictReader(file)
    for row in reader:
        delay_minutes = float(row["delay_minutes"])
        if delay_minutes <= 30.0:
            continue
        delayed_flights.append(row)
```

## Assignment

SnackStack has a CSV of device readings, but only some devices are relevant for the current analysis. You need to filter rows based on device characteristics.

**Complete the `filter_high_temperature_devices` function.** It accepts a list of device reading dictionaries and a temperature threshold.

2. [ ] Keep only the readings whose `temperature` is **greater than** the threshold.
3. [ ] Return the filtered list.

lessons.title: Writing CSV Files
lessons.readme:
# Writing CSV Files

Once you've read a CSV, you'll usually process it somehow, then write the result _back out_ in CSV.

The [`csv.DictWriter` class](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictWriter) writes a dictionary to a CSV file. Give it the output columns, write the header, then write rows:

```py
def save_attendance(filename: str, attendees: list[dict[str, str]]) -> None:
    fieldnames = ["name", "role", "checked_in"]

    with open(filename, "w", newline="") as file:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=fieldnames)
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(attendees)
```

- `fieldnames` decides the column order
- [`writeheader()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictWriter.writeheader) writes the first row
- [`writerows()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.csvwriter.writerows) writes many rows
- `newline=""` avoids blank-line weirdness on Windows

If you're generating results incrementally, the [`writerow()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.csvwriter.writerow) function can be used to write one row at a time in a loop:

```py
for attendee in attendees:
    writer.writerow(attendee)
```

For large datasets, it's more memory-efficient to work with files (both reading _and_ writing) by **streaming** rows instead of first collecting them in a list. Do you _really_ want to load a 20GB CSV directly into RAM? **Probably not.**

## Streaming Row by Row

This example opens both an input and output file, then reads, processes, and writes one row at a time:

```py
def stream_inventory_flags(input_file: str, output_file: str) -> None:
    with (
        open(input_file, "r", newline="") as in_f,
        open(output_file, "w", newline="") as out_f,
    ):
        reader = csv.DictReader(in_f)
        writer = csv.DictWriter(out_f, fieldnames=["sku", "needs_restock"])
        writer.writeheader()

        for row in reader:
            writer.writerow(
                {
                    "sku": row["sku"],
                    "needs_restock": int(row["quantity"]) < int(row["reorder_at"]),
                }
            )
```

This can handle _suuuuper_ large files. You're no longer limited by RAM, just by disk space.

## Assignment

**Complete the `export_temperature_summary` function.** It accepts a list of device dictionaries and writes a CSV at the provided path, with only `device_id` and `temperature`.

1. [ ] Use [`with open()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open) to open the file in write mode with `newline=""`.
2. [ ] Create a [`csv.DictWriter`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictWriter) with `fieldnames` _in this order_: `device_id`, `temperature`.
3. [ ] Write the header row first.
4. [ ] Write a summary row for each device, containing only the `device_id` and `temperature` fields.

def test_export_temperature_summary(
    devices: list[dict[str, str]], expected_lines: list[str]
) -> None:

    print("Devices:")
    pp(devices)
    output = CSVFile()
    try:
        with patch("builtins.open", return_value=output):
            export_temperature_summary(devices, "temperature_summary.csv")
        actual_lines = output.getvalue().strip().splitlines()
    except Exception as e:

        assert False

    print("\nExpected lines:")
    pp(expected_lines)
    print("\nActual lines:")
    pp(actual_lines)
    assert actual_lines == expected_lines

lessons.readme:
# Appending to CSV Files

Sometimes you want to create a brand-new CSV file, but sometimes you want to _keep_ the existing file and _append more rows to the end_.

If you open a file in [`"a"` (append) mode](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html#reading-and-writing-files), Python appends new content instead of overwriting the file:

```py
with open("posts.csv", "a", newline="") as file:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=["post_id", "likes", "published"])
    writer.writerow({"post_id": "post-12", "likes": "350", "published": "true"})
```

> [!danger]
> When appending, don't call [`writeheader()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictWriter.writeheader) again unless you're creating a brand-new file. You could wind up with duplicate headers in the middle of your CSV:
>
> ```csv
> post_id,likes,published
> post-01,1200,true
> post_id,likes,published
> post-12,350,true
> ```

## Assignment

The ops team has an existing CSV file with device data. You need to append new readings without overwriting what's already there.

**Complete the `append_multiple_readings` function.** It accepts a _list_ of device dictionaries and appends them to an existing CSV file at the provided path.

1. [ ] Use [`with open()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open) to open the file in append mode (`"a"`) with `newline=""`.
2. [ ] Use [`csv.DictWriter`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html#csv.DictWriter) with fieldnames _in this order_: `device_id`, `temperature`, `online`.
3. [ ] Write all the device rows, _not_ a header row.

lessons.title: What Is Pandas?
lessons.readme:
# What Is Pandas?

[Pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/) is the most popular Python library for data manipulation. It's _the_ tool for working with **tabular data** like spreadsheets, CSV files, and database tables.

> [!info]
> Later in this course we'll look at [Polars](https://pola.rs/), a newer alternative to Pandas that's quickly gaining popularity. But today, Pandas is still the dominant library.

Wes McKinney created Pandas in 2008 while working at a hedge fund to solve real-world data problems:

- Loading datasets from CSV, Excel, relational databases, APIs
- Filtering rows by conditions
- Creating new columns
- Grouping and aggregating
- Handling missing data
- Merging multiple datasets

Tasks that take many lines of code in Python become _one-liners_ with Pandas. They also tend to be _much_ faster, because Pandas relies on optimized, compiled array operations under the hood.

> [!miriah]
> If you're considering a career in data analytics, **Pandas is non-negotiable**. Data scientists, analysts, and even some backend engineers use it regularly.

Working with tabular data like spreadsheets, CSV files, and database tables
Creating web applications
Building machine learning models from scratch

lessons.title: Series
lessons.readme:
# Series

A **[`Series`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.html):** in Pandas is a one-dimensional labeled array (like a single column from a table)

If we had a spreadsheet of player data from an RPG, where each row represented a player, and each column represented some attribute about the player, **we could take any one of those columns as a Pandas `Series`**. For example, a column representing each player's `gold_earned`:

```py
import pandas as pd

gold_earned = pd.Series([150, 300, 75, 420])
print(gold_earned)
```

Prints:

```text
0    150
1    300
2     75
3    420
dtype: int64
```

- The **index labels** are on the left: `0, 1, 2, 3`
- The **values** are on the right: `150, 300, 75, 420`
- The **dtype** (data type) is at the bottom: `int64` (64-bit integer)

You can access an individual value by its index:

```py
print(gold_earned[0])  # 150
```

## When to Use a Series

You may be thinking, "Isn't this just a list?" Kinda... but the `Series` structure has advantages, most importantly:

- **Performance:** A `Series` uses optimized C-array operations under the hood, so it can be _much_ faster than the same operations on a regular Python list, especially at large sizes.
- **Powerful indexing:** A `Series` isn't just _ordered_ – it's _labeled_. That means you can manipulate data using custom labels instead of just integer positions. And if you perform an operation involving multiple `Series`, Pandas will automatically _align_ the data based on the index labels.

## Assignment

SnackStack tracks device telemetry data, including temperature readings from smart kitchen appliances. The analytics team needs to work with individual columns of data as `Series` to perform calculations.

**Complete the `get_temperature_stats` function.**

1. [ ] **Create a Pandas `Series`** from the `temperatures` list using [`pd.Series()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.html).
2. [ ] **Calculate the mean temperature** using the built-in Pandas [`.mean()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.mean.html) method.
3. [ ] **Calculate the maximum temperature** using the built-in Pandas [`.max()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.max.html) method.
4. [ ] **Return a dictionary** with keys `"mean"` and `"max"` containing the calculated values.

lessons.readme:
# DataFrames

While a `Series` represents a single column of data, a [`DataFrame`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html) is basically a **table** that can contain an arbitrary number of `Series` (columns).

It's essentially Pandas' version of an Excel spreadsheet, CSV file, or SQL table.

Say we have a _collection_ of a few columns that represent player data from an RPG:

```py
data = {
    "player": ["Geralt", "Ciri", "Triss"],
    "gold_earned": [150, 300, 75],
    "online": [True, False, True],
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)
```

Prints:

```text
   player  gold_earned  online
0  Geralt          150    True
1    Ciri          300   False
2   Triss           75    True
```

- The **index labels** are on the left: `0, 1, 2`
- The **column labels** are at the top: `player`, `gold_earned`, `online`
- The **values** are in the middle: the actual data for each player

`DataFrame`s are _everywhere_ in data manipulation; we'll be using these _a lot_.

> [!tip]
> We'll often use the variable name `df` as a concise way of representing a `DataFrame` in examples.

## Assignment

2. [ ] Assign that list to `data["status"]`.
3. [ ] Use [`pd.DataFrame()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html) to create a `DataFrame` from `data`, then return it.

> [!tip]
> Try printing the data _before_ and _after_ putting it in the `DataFrame` to see the difference in formatting!

lessons.title: Derived Columns
lessons.readme:
# Derived Columns

A **derived column** is a _new_ column calculated from columns you already have. You create one simply by assigning to a new column name. Pandas runs the operation across the _whole column at once_, no loop required:

```py
# df already contains a "subtotal" column
df["order_total"] = df["subtotal"] * 1.08 + 5
# now it also has an "order_total" column
```

It works like a spreadsheet formula that fills down every row. You can use any arithmetic, including combining multiple columns:

```py
# Adding a "discount" column by subtracting
# the "sale_price" column from "list_price" column
df["discount"] = df["list_price"] - df["sale_price"]
```

Of course, it also works with text. You can concatenate text with `+`, which is handy for building labels:

```py
# Add a "label" column by combining
# the "brand" and "category" columns with a hyphen in between
df["label"] = df["brand"] + "-" + df["category"]
```

> [!warning]
> Assigning to a column name that already exists _replaces_ that column instead of adding a new one.

## Assignment

SnackStack wants to flag how far each device drifts from its target temperature. **Complete the `add_temperature_deviation` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` with `"temperature"` and `"target_temperature"` columns, and returns it with an added `"temp_deviation"` column.

1. [ ] Subtract `"target_temperature"` from `"temperature"` to get each device's deviation.
2. [ ] Store the result, rounded to one decimal place with [`.round()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.round.html), in a new `"temp_deviation"` column.
3. [ ] Return the `DataFrame`.

lessons.title: Series vs. DataFrame
lessons.readme:
# Series vs. DataFrame

When you **select one column** from a `DataFrame`, you get a `Series`. Given the following `DataFrame`:

```text
        title   author  page_count
0  The Hobbit  Tolkien         310
1        Dune  Herbert         412
2          It     King        1138
```

We can select the `title` column:

```py
titles = df["title"]
print(titles)
```

Which prints the following `Series`:

```text
0    The Hobbit
1          Dune
2            It
Name: title, dtype: str
```

## Selecting Multiple Columns

When you **select multiple columns** from a `DataFrame`, you get another (smaller) `DataFrame`. We use double brackets here because we're actually passing a _list_ of column names as the key for selection:

```py
subset = df[["title", "page_count"]]
print(subset)
```

Which yields the following `DataFrame`:

```text
        title  page_count
0  The Hobbit         310
1        Dune         412
2          It        1138
```

**`Series` and `DataFrame` objects are not interchangeable.** They support different methods and properties, so keeping track of which one you have will help you avoid errors.

## Table vs. Column

Say we have a table of library books:

| book_id | title      | page_count | in_stock |
| ------- | ---------- | ---------- | -------- |
| 101     | The Hobbit | 310        | true     |
| 102     | Dune       | 412        | false    |
| 103     | It         | 1138       | true     |

- The **entire table** is a `DataFrame`.
- The **`title` column alone** is a `Series`.
- The **`page_count` column alone** is a `Series`.
- If we select **just the `title` and `in_stock` columns**, we'll have a smaller two-column `DataFrame`.

## Assignment

SnackStack's dashboard needs two slices of the same device table: a `Series` of device IDs, and an environment-panel `DataFrame`. The sensors report temperature in Fahrenheit, so a provided `add_celsius()` helper adds a `"temperature_c"` column for you.

**Complete the `get_device_views` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` and returns a tuple of two values.

1. [ ] Use the provided `add_celsius()` function to get a new `DataFrame` with a `"temperature_c"` column added.
2. [ ] Select the `"device_id"` column as a `Series`.
3. [ ] Select the `"temperature_c"` and `"humidity"` columns as a `DataFrame`.
4. [ ] Return the `Series` and the `DataFrame` in that order.

lessons.readme:
# Filtering Data

The standard way of filtering out specific rows in Pandas is **boolean indexing**. You put a boolean expression in the brackets, and Pandas keeps the rows where that expression evaluates to `True`.

> [!tip]
> "Boolean expression" means logic that can be applied to _each row_ to yield `True` or `False`.

Say you have a `DataFrame` of movie data, and you want a subset with only the films _rated above a certain score_:

```py
top_films = df[df["imdb_rating"] > 8.5]
print(top_films)
#            title   genre  imdb_rating     status
# 0  The Godfather   crime          9.2  streaming
# 2   Pulp Fiction   crime          8.9  streaming
# 4    Interstellar  sci-fi         8.7   archived
```

`top_films` is a new `DataFrame` with all the same _columns_, but we filtered it down to only the _rows_ that meet our condition.

> [!miriah]
> Pandas column comparisons like this are **vectorized** – they operate on entire columns at once, which is much faster than looping through rows individually!

The condition itself is just a `Series` of `True`/`False` values, one per row. You can store it in a variable and reuse it:

```py
# this is the same thing as above
is_top_film = df["imdb_rating"] > 8.5
top_films = df[is_top_film]
print(top_films)
```

Because `True` counts as `1` and `False` as `0`, calling [`.sum()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.sum.html) on that boolean `Series` tells you _how many_ rows match:

```py
top_count = int(is_top_film.sum())
print(top_count)
# 3
```

## Assignment

SnackStack's operations team needs to monitor device health. Smart fridges running too hot are a safety concern – nobody wants a spontaneous breakfast.

**Complete the `count_overheating_devices` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` of device readings and a temperature `threshold`. The operations dashboard wants the headline number _and_ the rows behind it, so it returns two values: the count of overheating devices and a `DataFrame` with just those rows.

1. [ ] Create a boolean condition (a `Series`) that is `True` where `temperature_celsius` is greater than `threshold`.
2. [ ] Use the condition to filter the `DataFrame` down to only the overheating devices.
3. [ ] Return two values: the [`.sum()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.sum.html) of the boolean condition, then the filtered `DataFrame`, in that order.

lessons.title: The Index in Pandas
lessons.readme:
# The Index in Pandas

Every `Series` and `DataFrame` has an **index** – a set of row labels, which appear on the left side when you print one of these structures. By default, Pandas assigns integer indexes starting at `0`:

```text
0    28
1    35
2    19
3    42
```

![Index in Pandas Explainer](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/Pandas_v2-1920x1080.mp4){captions="captions.vtt"}

## Not Just an Offset

The index isn't just a display nicety, nor is it a naïve row counter. It's a much more **flexible and powerful** means for Pandas to keep track of rows internally. Two important things to know:

1. **The index persists through filtering.** When you filter a `DataFrame` to keep only certain rows, the original index values come with those rows – they don't reset to `0, 1, 2...`. You might end up with index values like `1, 3, 7` after a filter.

   ```py
   # Original DataFrame has index 0, 1, 2
   df = pd.DataFrame(
       {
           "player": ["Curry", "Jokic", "Doncic"],
           "points": [22, 45, 50],
       }
   )

   # After filtering, index values are preserved
   big_games = df[df["points"] > 40]
   print(big_games)
   #    player  points
   # 1   Jokic      45
   # 2  Doncic      50
   ```

2. **You can reset the index** with [`.reset_index(drop=True)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.reset_index.html) to get a new `DataFrame` with a clean `0, 1, 2...` sequence after filtering.

   ```py
   big_games_reset = big_games.reset_index(drop=True)
   print(big_games_reset)
   #    player  points
   # 0   Jokic      45
   # 1  Doncic      50
   ```

> [!warning]
> If you call `reset_index` without setting `drop=True`, the old index becomes a _new column_ called `"index"`. Probably not what you want!

## Assignment

SnackStack's support team filters device data to find sensors that need attention:

```py
hot_devices = df[df["temperature"] > 80]
```

After filtering, the result keeps the **original index values**. That can leave the team with messy indexes like `5, 234, 891` in a tiny report.

**Complete the `reset_device_index` function.** It accepts a filtered `DataFrame` and should return a `DataFrame` with a fresh sequential index, plus a `"unique_idx"` label column built from that new index.

1. [ ] [Reset the index](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.reset_index.html), dropping the old index values.
2. [ ] Add a `"unique_idx"` column where each row's value is `"idx_"` followed by its new index number (so the first row is `"idx_0"`, the next `"idx_1"`, and so on). You can use the `DataFrame`'s [`.index` property](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.index.html) to get an iterable of its index values.
3. [ ] Return the updated `DataFrame`.

lessons.readme:
# Custom Indexes

While Pandas assigns integers as index labels by default – and that's often perfectly sufficient – you can also set **custom indexes**. This unlocks powerful features like [automatic alignment](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dsintro-alignment), where Pandas matches rows by label instead of position.

## Setting a Custom Index

If you have a column in a `DataFrame` that contains a unique identifier for each row, you can use that column as the index by calling the [`.set_index()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.set_index.html):

```py
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "flight": ["UA123", "DL456", "AA789"],
        "destination": ["Denver", "Atlanta", "Dallas"],
        "delay_minutes": [12, 0, 45],
    }
)

df = df.set_index("flight")
print(df)
#        destination  delay_minutes
# flight
# UA123       Denver             12
# DL456      Atlanta              0
# AA789       Dallas             45
```

Now rows are identified directly by the flight number (`UA123`, `DL456`...) instead of by sequential integers.

You can select rows directly using [`.loc[]`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.loc.html) with the index labels:

```py
print(df.loc["UA123"])
# destination      Denver
# delay_minutes        12
# Name: UA123, dtype: object
```

## Common Index Types

Two types of column that are often used for custom indexes are **strings**, like a product SKU:

```py
products = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "sku": ["BOOK-HIST-HC-9781", "JCKT-DNM-BLU-L", "LAMP-DSK-LED-WHT"],
        "price": [19.99, 29.99, 9.99],
        "stock": [100, 50, 200],
    }
).set_index("sku")

print(products)
#                    price  stock
# sku
# BOOK-HIST-HC-9781  19.99    100
# JCKT-DNM-BLU-L     29.99     50
# LAMP-DSK-LED-WHT    9.99    200
```

Though another common one is _timestamps_, which we'll cover later in the course.

## Assignment

SnackStack's device registry has no single unique ID column, but each device's `device_type` and `location` are unique _in combination_. The support team wants to build a key from those two columns and use it as the index.

**Complete the `set_device_index` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` and should return a new `DataFrame` indexed by a combined `"device_key"`.

1. [ ] Build a `"device_key"` column by joining each row's `"device_type"` and `"location"` with a `-` (so a kitchen fridge becomes `"fridge-kitchen"`).
2. [ ] Set `"device_key"` as the index with [`.set_index()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.set_index.html), then return the result.

lessons.readme:
# Loading Data

We've set up a few small example `DataFrame`s in code, but real data usually comes from _files_, which, as you know, need to be loaded.

For CSV data, Pandas offers the [`pd.read_csv()` function](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html) function, which loads a CSV file directly into a `DataFrame`:

```py
df = pd.read_csv("stream_history.csv")
```

That's it! One line of code loads your entire dataset into a convenient form in memory.

Pandas is also smart enough to use the first row of the CSV as column headers, so you don't have to worry about that (as long as the file is well-formed).

## Read Row by Row

Sometimes reading a massive file into memory isn't what you want. Maybe you're on a machine with limited RAM, and you're trying to work with a `25GB` CSV file. The `chunksize` parameter lets you read the file in smaller `DataFrame` chunks:

```py
# will read 100 lines into a DataFrame at a time
chunk_size_num_lines = 100

for chunk in pd.read_csv("large_file.csv", chunksize=chunk_size_num_lines):
    # do stuff with each dataframe...
    process_chunk(chunk)
```

## Assignment

SnackStack's kitchen sensors export daily readings to CSV files. We need to get them imported as Pandas `DataFrame`s for analysis.

**Complete the `load_device_data` function.** It accepts a CSV file path and returns a `DataFrame` with the file's contents.

1. [ ] Use [`pd.read_csv()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html) to load the CSV file.
2. [ ] Convert the `"timestamp"` column to datetime objects with [`pd.to_datetime()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.to_datetime.html) before returning the `DataFrame`.

lessons.readme:
# Inspect Head

_Never_ start manipulating data without inspecting it first. In the real world, data gets messy. Inspection reveals:

- Missing values that could break your analysis
- Wrong data types (e.g., numbers stored as text)
- Unexpected values (negative prices, dates far in the future)
- Inconsistent column names

Skipping inspection leads to bugs that are hard to track down later.

**The [`.head()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.head.html) is straightforward**: it returns a new `DataFrame` with _just_ the first few rows. Use this to get a quick look at your data's shape, to see if it even makes sense.

```py
head_df = df.head()  # Returns the first 5 rows (default setting)
print(head_df)
```

Which prints something like this:

```text
         dish  price        ordered_at
0   Carbonara   16.5  2024-03-02 18:30
1  Margherita   12.0  2024-03-02 18:45
2    Tiramisu    7.5  2024-03-02 19:00
3  Bruschetta    6.0  2024-03-02 19:15
4     Negroni   11.0  2024-03-02 19:30
```

You can optionally pass a number to `.head()` to get a different number of rows:

```py
df.head(10)  # Returns the first 10 rows
```

## Assignment

SnackStack's operations team sometimes needs a quick sample of incoming sensor data before processing a full batch. **Complete the `preview_devices` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` and a row count `n`, and returns the first `n` rows with only the `"device_id"` and `"temperature"` columns.

2. [ ] Select just the `"device_id"` and `"temperature"` columns, then return the result.

lessons.readme:
# Info & Describe

The [`.head()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.head.html) method is good for a quick "sniff test" of a new `DataFrame`, but you'll also want to look at **summary info** about the data. This is where the `.info()` and `.describe()` methods come in.

## Info

The [`.info()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.info.html) prints a concise summary of your `DataFrame`.

```py
df.info()
```

Prints something like this:

```text
<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 20 entries, 0 to 19
Data columns (total 3 columns):
 #   Column  Non-Null Count  Dtype
---  ------  --------------  -----
 0   city    20 non-null     str
 1   price   20 non-null     float64
 2   sqft    19 non-null     float64
dtypes: float64(2), str(1)
memory usage: 472.0 bytes
```

We get a _bunch_ of useful info at once:

- The **number of rows** (in this example, `20`)
- The **number of columns** (`3`)
- The **column names** and their **data types** (`str`, `float64`)
- The **count of non-null values** in each column (`sqft` has `19` non-null, meaning `1` missing value)
- The **memory footprint** of the `DataFrame` (`472.0 bytes`)

## Describe

The [`.describe()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.describe.html) digs a bit deeper, generating descriptive statistics for numeric columns by default:

```py
stats_df = df.describe()
print(stats_df)
```

This `return`s a new `DataFrame` containing the statistics. If you `print` it, the output will look something like this:

```text
               price         sqft
count      20.000000    19.000000
mean   470250.000000  1575.263158
std    150939.818959   410.573696
min    225000.000000   880.000000
25%    373750.000000  1325.000000
50%    465000.000000  1550.000000
75%    548750.000000  1825.000000
max    815000.000000  2400.000000
```

- **`count`:** Number of non-null (non-missing) values
- **`mean`:** Average value
- **`std`:** Standard deviation (how spread out the values are; higher = more variation)
- **`min`:** Minimum (smallest) value
- **`25%`:** First quartile (25% of values are _below_ this)
- **`50%`:** Median (middle value; half of values are above, half below)
- **`75%`:** Third quartile (75% of values are _below_ this)
- **`max`:** Maximum (largest) value

Because `.describe()` returns a `DataFrame`, you can select from it like any other `DataFrame`. The [`.loc[]` indexer](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.loc.html) selects by **label** instead of numeric position.

```py
stats = df.describe()
price_stats = stats["price"]
print(price_stats.loc["mean"])
# 470250.0
```

## Assignment

SnackStack's analytics team needs the average temperature for a new batch of sensor readings, after a quick structural check. **Complete the `get_average_temperature` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame`, prints its info, and returns the mean temperature.

1. [ ] Print the `DataFrame`'s info with [`.info()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.info.html).
2. [ ] Get the descriptive statistics with [`.describe()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.describe.html).
3. [ ] Select the `"temperature"` column from the stats, grab its `"mean"` with [`.loc[]`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.loc.html), and return that rounded to two decimal places.

lessons.title: Inspecting Workflow
lessons.readme:
# Inspecting Workflow

When you're inspecting a new dataset, here's what "good data" looks like:

1. **Reasonable null counts** – A few missing values are normal, but if 50% of a column is null, that's usually a problem.
2. **Expected data types** – Numbers should use an appropriate numeric type, not `object` (i.e., text).
3. **Realistic min/max values** – Negative ages? Dates in the year 2200? Investigate.
4. **Consistent column names** – If you see `user_id` and `userId`, something's off.
5. **Expected row counts** – Does the number of rows match what you were told about the data?

Real-world data is often messy, so you need to know what you're dealing with. If you see any of the issues mentioned above, it's a sign that **you need to do some data cleaning** before you can conduct any meaningful analysis.

> [!miriah]
> When I start working with a dataset, after loading it into a `DataFrame`, the first thing I do is run [`.head()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.head.html), [`.info()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.info.html), and [`.describe()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.describe.html) _in that order_. For example:
>
> 1. **I get a new dataset for last month's sales**.
> 2. **I run `.head()`** – "Okay, the columns make sense."
> 3. **I run `.info()`** – "Hmm, 500 null values in the email column seems weird."
> 4. **I run `.describe()`** – "Wait, the mean price is negative? Must be a bug..."

lessons.readme:
# Data Properties

In addition to the methods we just covered, `DataFrame`s have a few useful properties for figuring out what's inside:

- The [`.shape` property](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.shape.html) returns a tuple of the number of rows and columns in the `DataFrame`.
- The [`.columns` property](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.columns.html) returns the names of the columns.
- The [`.dtypes` property](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.dtypes.html) returns the data types of each column.

```py
df = pd.read_csv("posts.csv")

print(df.shape)
# (997, 3)

print(df.columns)
# Index(['username', 'engagement_rate', 'platform'], dtype='str')

print(df.dtypes)
# username               str
# engagement_rate    float64
# platform               str
# dtype: object
```

In the example above, we have:

- A `DataFrame` with `997` rows and `3` columns
- Columns named `username` (`str`), `engagement_rate` (`float64`), and `platform` (`str`)

You can get similar context by calling the [`.info()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.info.html) method, but these individual properties are convenient when you only need one piece of metadata.

## Assignment

When the SnackStack analytics team receives a new device dataset, they need to quickly understand its structure before diving into analysis.

**Complete the `get_device_metadata` function to return a new dictionary** with these keys:

1. [ ] `"shape"`: the `DataFrame`'s [`.shape`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.shape.html).
2. [ ] `"row_count"`: the number of rows from `.shape`.
3. [ ] `"column_count"`: the number of columns from `.shape`.
4. [ ] `"columns"`: the column names as a _list_ (wrap [`.columns`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.columns.html) with [`list()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#func-list)).
5. [ ] `"dtypes"`: the column data types from [`.dtypes`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.dtypes.html), left as a `Series`.

# Inspecting Columns

Once you understand your `DataFrame` as a whole, you can inspect individual `Series` (columns) with a few more tools:

- The [`.unique()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.unique.html) returns an array of the unique values in a `Series`.
- The [`.value_counts()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.value_counts.html) returns a `Series` containing _counts_ of unique values.

```py
df = pd.read_csv("games.csv")

print(df["genre"].unique())
# <StringArray>
# ['RPG', 'Shooter', 'Puzzle']
# Length: 3, dtype: str

print(df["genre"].value_counts())
# genre
# RPG        150
# Shooter    120
# Puzzle      80
# Name: count, dtype: int64
```

In the example above, there are:

- 3 unique values in the `"genre"` column
- 150 rows where `"genre"` is `"RPG"`, 120 rows where it's `"Shooter"`, etc.

> [!tip]
> The `.value_counts()` method lists results in _descending_ order by default.

3. [ ] Return the unique types and the counts as a tuple, in that order.

lessons.title: Multiple Conditions
lessons.readme:
# Multiple Conditions

Real-world filtering rarely involves just one condition. Pandas lets you combine conditions using the logical operators `&` ("and") and `|` ("or").

## AND Condition

Say I want to filter for basketball players averaging between `20` and `30` points per game:

```py
solid_scorers = df[(df["ppg"] >= 20.0) & (df["ppg"] <= 30.0)]
print(solid_scorers)
#             player     team   ppg    status
# 0     Jayson Tatum  Celtics  26.9    active
# 13    Devin Booker     Suns  27.1    active
# 15    Jrue Holiday  Celtics  21.4   injured
```

> [!danger]
> Each condition must be wrapped in its own parentheses when combined: `(condition_1) & (condition_2)`. Leaving them out causes a Python operator precedence error.

## Don't Confuse Operators

**In Pandas, always use `&` and `|` instead of `and` and `or`.**

We can't use the regular Python logical operators because they work with single `True`/`False` values. When filtering a `DataFrame`, we're comparing entire `Series` at once.

## OR Condition

Say we want the records for players at the extremes – either bench warmers (under `5` ppg) _or_ superstars (over `35` ppg):

```py
extreme_scorers = df[(df["ppg"] < 5) | (df["ppg"] > 35)]
print(extreme_scorers)
#               player       team   ppg  status
# 4        Joel Embiid      76ers  35.3  active
# 9   Payton Pritchard    Celtics   4.1  active
# 16       Luka Doncic  Mavericks  38.7  active
```

You can mix `&` and `|` in a single filter – just keep each piece wrapped in parentheses so the grouping is clear.

## Assignment

SnackStack's support team knows a device needs a technician's attention when it's online and _either_ a fridge running too warm _or_ an oven running too cold.

**Complete the `find_devices_needing_attention` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` of device readings and returns only the rows that need attention.

The `DataFrame` has `device_id`, `device_type`, `temperature_celsius`, and `status` columns.

1. [ ] Create a new `DataFrame`, keeping only the rows that have an "online" status AND _either_ a "fridge" (`device_type`) warmer than `5.0` (`temperature_celsius`) OR an "oven" colder than `150.0`.
2. [ ] Return the result.

lessons.title: The Not Operator
lessons.readme:
# The Not Operator

What about _negating_ a boolean mask? In Pandas, you use **the `~` operator**, though direct comparisons can still use `!=`.

```py
# Tracks that are NOT available
unavailable = df[~(df["status"] == "available")]

# Available tracks that are NOT in the US market
available_not_us = df[(df["status"] == "available") & ~(df["market"] == "US")]
```

The `~` **flips** boolean values – `True` becomes `False` and _vice versa_.

> [!miriah]
> Just like `&` and `|`, wrap the thing you're negating in parentheses: `~(df["market"] == "US")`. It keeps the precedence unambiguous.

## Assignment

The West Coast SnackStack team wants to monitor every device _outside_ their own region – but only the ones that are still reachable.

1. [ ] Create a new `DataFrame`, keeping only
   1. [ ] The rows that are NOT in the given `region`...
   2. [ ] AND those whose `status` is NOT "offline".
2. [ ] Return the result.

lessons.readme:
# Filter Methods

Pandas provides convenient built-in methods for common filtering operations. Each one returns a boolean `Series` you can use to index a `DataFrame`.

The [`.isin()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.isin.html) method checks whether each value in a column appears in a given list:

```py
target_platforms = df[df["platform"].isin(["PS5", "Switch"])]
```

The [`.between()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.between.html) method checks whether values fall within a range (inclusive by default):

```py
mid_priced = df[df["price"].between(20, 40)]
```

The [`.notnull()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.notnull.html) method returns `True` wherever a value is present (not missing):

```py
rated_games = df[df["metascore"].notnull()]
```

## Assignment

SnackStack is about to push a firmware update over the air. To avoid bricking devices, ops only wants to target devices that are **in a rollout region**, have **reported a temperature recently**, and have a **battery level in a safe range**.

**Complete the `get_update_targets` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame`, a list of rollout `regions`, and a `min_battery`/`max_battery` range, and returns only the devices safe to update.

1. 2. [ ] Return the result.

lessons.title: Binning
lessons.readme:
# Binning

"Binning" means grouping _continuous_ numbers into _discrete_ categories. Say you have some temperature readings, you could "bin" them into three categories: "Cold", "Normal", and "Hot":

![binning example](courses/diagrams/ca91a92b-c974-471e-a0b3-43e6778864a0/binning.svg)

Other examples include:

- Instead of raw test scores, you could "bin" them into the letter grades `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, and `F`.
- Instead of raw star ratings (`3.2`, `4.7`...), you could use tiers (`Low`, `Mid`, `Top`).

So, why bin your data?

- It **simplifies analysis** (patterns are easier to see in groups).
- It creates **segments** for business decisions.
- It **reduces noise** in the data.

The [`pd.cut()` function](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.cut.html) is an easy way to create "bins" in a `DataFrame`.

Here we create a new `rating_tier` column set to `"Low"`, `"Mid"`, or `"Top"` based on the `rating` column:

```py
# 0 up to 3 = Low
# above 3 up to 4 = Mid
# above 4 up to 5 = Top
df["rating_tier"] = pd.cut(
    df["rating"],
    bins=[0, 3, 4, 5],
    labels=["Low", "Mid", "Top"],
    include_lowest=True,
)
```

> [!tip]
> The `include_lowest=True` argument makes sure the very first edge (`0`) is included in the lowest bin.

## Assignment

SnackStack's support team wants a quick categorical view of the device fleet for their dashboard: a temperature zone and a battery tier for every device.

**Complete the `categorize_devices` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` of devices and returns a copy with two new categorical columns.

1. [ ] Create a [`df.copy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.copy.html) to work with so you don't mutate the original `DataFrame`.
2. [ ] Add a `temp_zone` column to the copy by [binning](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.cut.html) `temperature_celsius`:
   - "Cold" (up to 5°C)
   - "Normal" (above 5 up to 25°C)
   - "Hot" (above 25°C).
   - (Be sure to include the lowest edge in the first bin)
     > [!tip]
     > Use `float("-inf")` and `float("inf")` when the values are unbounded
3. [ ] Add a `battery_tier` column by binning `battery_level`:
   - "Low" (up to 20)
   - "Medium" (above 20 up to 60)
   - "High" (above 60 up to 100).
   - (Be sure to include the lowest edge in the first bin)
4. [ ] Return the updated copy of the `DataFrame`.

lessons.title: String Operations
lessons.readme:
# String Operations

Text data is _especially messy_. Restaurant names don't follow a consistent format, cuisines are typed by hand, menu items drift... it never ends.

Fortunately, Pandas [`.str` methods](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.html) let you transform text columns efficiently. You'll often need to:

- **Standardize case** – `"TACOS"`, `"Tacos"`, and `"tacos"` should all match
- **Remove whitespace** – `" Los Pollos Hermanos "` should be `"Los Pollos Hermanos"`
- **Replace text** – swap spaces for hyphens in every restaurant name
- **Extract patterns** – pull the domain out of a reservation email

Leaving text data in a dirty state causes incorrect groupings, failed joins, and misleading reports!

## Common String Methods

- Applying **uppercase**, **lowercase**, or **title case**:
  ```py
  df["restaurant"].str.upper()  # ALL CAPS
  df["restaurant"].str.lower()  # all lowercase
  df["city"].str.title()  # Title Case
  ```
- Removing **leading/trailing whitespace**:
  ```py
  # " Los Pollos Hermanos " becomes "Los Pollos Hermanos"
  df["restaurant"].str.strip()
  ```
- **Replacing text:**
  ```py
  # Replace spaces with hyphens
  df["restaurant"].str.replace(" ", "-", regex=False)
  ```
- Checking if a string **contains** a given substring:
  ```py
  # Returns a boolean Series
  df["cuisine"].str.contains("taco")
  ```
- **Splitting** strings into parts:
  ```py
  # Split a reservation email at the @ symbol
  df["email"].str.split("@")  # Returns a Series of lists
  df["email"].str.split("@").str[1]  # Returns a Series of just the domain parts
  ```

## Chaining

Because each `.str` method returns a new `Series`, you can **chain** them to apply several transformations in a row:

```py
df["restaurant"].str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(" ", "-", regex=False)
```

## Assignment

**Complete the `clean_device_registry` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` and returns a copy with two cleaned-up columns.

1. [ ] Create a [`df.copy()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.copy.html) to work with so you don't mutate the original `DataFrame`.
2. [ ] Add a `clean_id` column. It should be the `device_id`, but have [leading/trailing whitespace removed](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.strip.html), [all lowercase text](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.lower.html), and [replace inner spaces with hyphens (`-`)](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.replace.html).
3. [ ] Add a `clean_location` column. It should be the `location`, but have leading/trailing whitespace removed and [be in title case](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.title.html).
4. [ ] Return the updated `DataFrame`.

lessons.readme:
# Filtering With String Methods

Predicate `.str` methods like these return boolean `Series`, which means you can use them to **filter** a `DataFrame` just like a numeric comparison. If the source can contain missing values, pass `na=False` or handle them first.

```py
# Flights whose number contains "UA"
united = df[df["flight_number"].str.contains("UA")]

# Flights whose number starts with "DL"
delta = df[df["flight_number"].str.startswith("DL")]

# Flights whose route ends with "-JFK"
to_jfk = df[df["route"].str.endswith("-JFK")]
```

- [`.str.contains(sub)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.contains.html) – `True` if the substring appears anywhere
- [`.str.startswith(prefix)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.startswith.html) – `True` if the string starts with `prefix`
- [`.str.endswith(suffix)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.str.endswith.html) – `True` if the string ends with `suffix`

## Case Sensitivity

`.str.contains()` is **case-sensitive** by default, so `"DELAYED"` won't match `"delayed"`. Pass `case=False` to match regardless of case:

```py
# Matches "delayed", "Delayed", "DELAYED", etc.
df[df["status"].str.contains("delayed", case=False)]
```

## Combining String Filters

Just like numeric conditions, you can combine string conditions with `&` and `|`:

```py
# Delta flights that are currently delayed
df[
    df["flight_number"].str.startswith("DL")
    & df["status"].str.contains("delayed", case=False)
]
```

2. [ ] Return the result.

lessons.title: Sorting Data
lessons.readme:
# Sorting Data

Pandas provides a convenient [`.sort_values()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sort_values.html) to sort a `DataFrame` by column values.

```py
# Sort by a single column (ascending by default)
df_sorted = df.sort_values("price")

# Sort in descending order
df_sorted = df.sort_values("price", ascending=False)
```

You can **get the top N rows** by chaining [`.head()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.head.html) after sorting:

```py
# 10 most expensive listings
priciest = df.sort_values("price", ascending=False).head(10)

# 5 cheapest listings
cheapest = df.sort_values("price").head(5)
```

## Sorting by Multiple Columns

To sort by multiple columns, pass a _list_ of column names. Pandas sorts by the first column, then breaks ties with the next:

```py
# Sort by type first, then by price within each type
df_sorted = df.sort_values(["property_type", "price"])

# Mix ascending and descending
df_sorted = df.sort_values(
    ["property_type", "price"],
    ascending=[True, False],  # type A–Z, then price high–low
)
```

> [!miriah]
> A second sort column is great for **deterministic tie-breaking**. If two listings have the same price, sorting by `listing_id` next guarantees the same order every time.

## Assignment

SnackStack's field technicians can only service so many devices per shift. The support team wants a **triage list**: the `n` hottest devices first, so the riskiest units get attention soonest.

**Complete the `get_triage_list` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` and a count `n`, and returns the top `n` devices to service.

1. [ ] [Sort](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sort_values.html) the `DataFrame` by `temperature_celsius` (descending), breaking ties by `device_id` (ascending).
2. [ ] Take the first `n` rows with [`.head(n)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.head.html) and return the result.

lessons.readme:
# More Sorting

The [`.sort_index()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sort_index.html) sorts a `DataFrame` by its _index_ (the row labels) instead of by a column's values.

After filtering, those labels are often out of order. Sorting by index is also particularly handy when you've set a custom index like string IDs or timestamps.

```py
# Sort by index
df_sorted = df.sort_index()

# Sort by index in descending order
df_sorted = df.sort_index(ascending=False)
```

## In-Place Sorting

By default, `.sort_values()` returns a _new_ `DataFrame`. Pass `inplace=True` to modify the original instead:

```py
df.sort_values("close_price", inplace=True)
```

## Handling Missing Values

Real market data has gaps. You can control where `NaN` ("[Not a Number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NaN)") values land in the sorted output:

```py
# NaN values at the end (the default)
df_sorted = df.sort_values("close_price", na_position="last")

# NaN values at the beginning
df_sorted = df.sort_values("close_price", na_position="first")
```

This matters any time you sort by a numeric column that has missing values.

## Assignment

SnackStack's field technicians need a daily service route. Devices that **failed to report a temperature** (a `NaN` reading) are the most suspicious, and everything else follows, hottest first.

**Complete the `build_service_route` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` and returns a `DataFrame` ordered for the technician's route.

[Sort](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.sort_values.html) by `temperature_celsius` in descending order with `NaN`s positioned first.

lessons.title: Conditional Updates
lessons.readme:
# Conditional Updates

Filtering creates a new `DataFrame` containing only the rows that match a condition. But sometimes you may want to _keep all_ rows while _updating some_ of them.

For this, we can use [`.loc[]`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.loc.html) with a boolean mask and a column name:

```py
needs_service = df["battery_level"] < 20
df.loc[needs_service, "status"] = "needs service"
```

The first input to `.loc[]` is a mask that selects rows with `battery_level` under `20`; the second input selects the `status` column as the one to update. Rows with a low battery level will get a `status` of `"needs service"`, while other rows are left unchanged.

> [!warning]
> Assigning through `.loc[]` modifies the `DataFrame` directly. If you need to preserve the original data, create a copy before updating rows.

## Update Operations

You can also perform an operation on the selected values. For example, to increment the count of connection retries for offline devices:

```py
is_offline = df["status"] == "offline"
df.loc[is_offline, "retry_count"] += 1
```

> [!warning]
> Don't try to do this with a chained assignment like `df[is_offline]["retry_count"] += 1`. The first selection produces a temporary `DataFrame`, so the update never reaches `df`. Pandas will also emit a [`ChainedAssignmentError` warning](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.errors.ChainedAssignmentError.html).

## Assignment

SnackStack's devices report energy usage in mixed units: some use watt-hours (`"Wh"`), while others use [kilowatt-hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilowatt-hour) (`"kWh"`). The analytics team needs every reading in kilowatt-hours. `1` kilowatt-hour is equal to `1000` watt-hours.

**Complete the `normalize_energy_units` function.** It accepts a `DataFrame` with `device_id`, `energy_usage`, and `energy_unit` columns. The `energy_usage` values are floats, and each `energy_unit` is either `"Wh"` or `"kWh"`. The function should return a new `DataFrame` with all energy readings expressed in kilowatt-hours.

1. [ ] Create a [copy](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.copy.html) of the `DataFrame` to avoid modifying the original.
2. [ ] Create a boolean mask that identifies rows where `energy_unit` is `"Wh"`.
3. [ ] Use the mask with `.loc[]` to divide the `energy_usage` values in those rows by `1000`.
4. [ ] Use the same mask with `.loc[]` to update `energy_unit` in those rows to `"kWh"`.
5. [ ] Return the updated `DataFrame`.
